scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that distance can sharpen understanding, then argues we still learn from the past in the present; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: It is often said that we understand events only long after they have passed.
One claim holds that knowing about the past cannot help us decide today, on the reason that we cannot connect current and past events until we have distance from both.
I disagree with the claim, because we can and do learn from the past even while living through the present.
First, there is some truth in the idea that distance helps us understand events.
Looking back calmly, we can often see causes and patterns that were hidden in the moment.
For example, the full meaning of a war or a crisis often becomes clear only years afterward.
This shows that time can indeed sharpen our understanding of what has happened.
In the heat of events, strong feelings can blur our judgment of what is really going on.
Some lessons of history truly do become clearer with the passing of years.
To this extent, the reason behind the claim holds a grain of truth.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why the past still helps now

sentences.text: Second, however, we do not need full distance to learn useful lessons from the past.
Well-understood events from long ago can guide our choices in the present right now.
Consider how leaders today study past wars and crises to avoid repeating old mistakes.
Such use of history shows that the past helps us act wisely even in the present moment.
We can also learn from our own earlier mistakes without waiting many years to do so.
Waiting for perfect distance would leave us helpless whenever a decision could not wait.
The past, then, can guide us today even before we have full distance from it.
In conclusion, distance from events can certainly deepen our understanding of them.
But we do not need that distance to draw useful lessons from the past today.
History helps us decide wisely in the present, even while the present is still unfolding.
